clinicalPearls: Follows blunt or penetrating head and orbital trauma, classically frontal or brow impact that transmits force to the tightly tethered intracanalicular optic nerve.
Distinguish direct injury, such as nerve laceration, avulsion, bony fragment or sheath haematoma, from indirect injury from deceleration and shearing forces.
There is acute visual loss with a relative afferent pupillary defect, while the disc is often normal at onset and becomes pale after several weeks.
It is commonly associated with maxillofacial and orbital fractures and closed head injury and may be masked in an unconscious patient.
Computed tomography of the orbits and optic canal with fine cuts is central to assessment, identifying fractures, haematoma and nerve impingement.
Management is controversial and includes observation, high-dose corticosteroids or optic canal decompression, with no proven benefit from routine steroids.
High-dose corticosteroids are potentially harmful in the setting of significant head injury, as shown in major head-injury trials.
An orbital compartment syndrome from retrobulbar haemorrhage is a treatable emergency requiring urgent lateral canthotomy and cantholysis.
reference.pathophysiology: Traumatic optic neuropathy involves both primary and secondary mechanisms. Primary injury results from direct disruption of axons or from mechanical force transmitted to the firmly anchored intracanalicular segment, where the nerve is least able to dissipate energy. Secondary injury then evolves within the confined bony optic canal through oedema, ischaemia, oxidative stress and apoptotic cell death, causing progressive axonal loss. A retrobulbar haemorrhage can additionally compress the nerve and its blood supply, producing a compartment-type ischaemic insult.
additionalDifferentials: Orbital compartment syndrome from retrobulbar haemorrhage
Globe rupture or severe anterior segment injury
additionalInvestigations: Computed tomography of the head and orbits with dedicated fine optic canal views
Assessment of visual acuity and pupils for a relative afferent pupillary defect
Colour vision testing and visual fields when the patient is able to cooperate
Measurement of intraocular pressure and assessment for proptosis and a tense orbit
Magnetic resonance imaging when a sheath haematoma or soft-tissue injury is suspected
Optical coherence tomography of the retinal nerve fibre layer at follow-up
redFlags: Proptosis with raised intraocular pressure and a tense orbit indicating a compartment syndrome needing emergency canthotomy
Bilateral visual loss or no perception of light
reference.prognosis: Outcome is variable; poor prognostic features include no perception of light at presentation, an optic canal fracture, older age and loss of consciousness. Some patients recover useful vision spontaneously.
pitfalls: Missing the diagnosis in an unconscious or multiply injured patient
Administering high-dose corticosteroids in significant head injury despite evidence of harm
Overlooking a treatable retrobulbar haemorrhage requiring urgent orbital decompression
Delaying surgical decompression when a clear compressive lesion is present
management: Relieve orbital compartment pressure emergently with lateral canthotomy and cantholysis when a retrobulbar haemorrhage threatens the nerve
Consider observation, high-dose corticosteroids or optic canal decompression on an individualised basis, recognising that routine steroids are of unproven benefit
Image the head and orbits with fine-cut CT of the optic canal to identify fracture, haematoma or nerve impingement amenable to surgery
Undertake surgical decompression of the optic canal or evacuation of a compressive sheath haematoma in selected cases with impingement
Serially monitor visual acuity, pupillary responses and colour vision to track the afferent defect and treatment response
Manage jointly with neuro-ophthalmology and maxillofacial or orbital surgery, alongside treatment of associated head and facial injuries
